name: Brick Red
lede: Brick Red is a color named for a building material, used by naturalists and dictionary-makers long before it became a paint-chart name, and its screen swatch is much pinker than any brick.

sections.title: A color named for a thing
sections.body:
Paterson defines brick as the deep orange-red of brick, and brick-red as the color of red brick, adding that in the United States it means a brownish or yellowish red [1]. That is a real disagreement over the word: the British sense is orange-leaning, the American one browner and duller [1]. The dictionary also gives older, learned equivalents, *lateritious* and *testaceous* (the last described as the reddish-brown of unglazed tiles or flowerpots) [1].

The name is old in the lists of naturalists. In the chart published by Schäffer in 1769, number 76, brick red, was a mixture of minium, lead white, orpiment and English red [2]. Brick-red then sits among the reds in the Werner-family lists reproduced by Baty, those of Lenz, Widenmann and Syme among them [3]. When Jameson revised Werner's terms in the early 1800s he renamed it tile red, a change Syme's 1821 list echoes [4]. Maerz and Paul's 1930 dictionary dates the English color word to 1667 [5].

Garfield, reporting a tally of about 7,500 English color names, files brick red among the 149 taken from common things, far behind the 528 flowers [6]. Most names, in other words, borrow from something people already knew by sight.

sections.title: Which brick red
sections.body:
The swatch here, #CB4154, is a strong crimson-leaning red, and Wikipedia's version of it cites Crayola [5]. Ridgway's 1912 *Color Standards and Color Nomenclature* shows a much browner, darker Brick Red, near #915248, which is closer to the word as Paterson's American sense describes it [5]. The nearest named color to the swatch is [[cerise]], 5.5 units away, and a RAL paint, strawberry red (RAL 3018), is practically the same screen color [5]. Real fired brick sits closer to the colors we name [[brick]] and [[terracotta]].

So the name and the swatch have drifted apart. Read the swatch as a bright red filed under a familiar word, and keep Ridgway's browner color in mind as the brick it was named for [5].

sections.title: In dye, paint and cloth
sections.body:
Madder dyeing was unreliable. Greenfield notes that madder reds tended toward orange, and that dyers often ended with corals, russets and brick reds [7]. Only dyers in the Ottoman Empire, India and other Eastern countries could consistently get a rich red, the Turkey red of Europe, a process of more than a dozen steps over three or four months [7].

Brick red meant something else to the pigment trade: brick dust was a known cheat. Cennino advised buying vermilion in one unbroken lump because apothecaries diluted it with red lead or brick dust [8], and indigo was adulterated with brick dust too [9]. Riffault described a dark brick-red mercury chromate in 1874, and Salter in 1869 said red precipitate could be made in brick-red or orange-yellow forms [10].

In nineteenth-century dress it was a respectable color. English fashion manuals condemned scarlet and crimson as vulgar, but allowed a married lady dark reds, brick reds and maroon [11]. Some dictionaries have kin: Morocco is a brick red that was originally the color of painted leather, and Pompeian red is a dark brick red named for the houses found at Pompeii [12]. Our nearest named neighbor of that kind is [[pompeian-red]].

sections.title: Where to look
sections.body:
Brick shows one of the best-known lessons about color context. Albers described a student's demonstration that the same light red bricks look much lighter with white mortar than with black [13]. The Symbolist painter Sérusier thought warm and cool colors could not share a composition, and once told the dealer Ambroise Vollard that a violet coat beside Vollard's brick-colored overcoat made the two colors scream [14].

In medicine, Birren quotes a nineteenth-century style of listing in which a brick-red face goes with Osler's disease in warm weather [15]. Read it as a period diagnostic habit, not as evidence about the color.

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body:
In our archive of 23,781 paintings, a color within six units of this swatch covers at least five per cent of the canvas in 12 works, or 0.05 per cent [16]. The earliest is Gillis Peeters's *Watermill by a Wooded Outcrop*, of 1633, at 5.2 per cent [16]. Bonnard's *The Red Blouse*, of 1925, reaches 12.4 per cent [16].

The surprise is where it clusters. Seven of the 12 are Kalighat paintings from Calcutta, a movement with 7 hits in 96 works; the three largest, at 15 to 20 per cent each, are Kalighat gods and heroes from about 1890 [16]. That makes India the leading country, 7 of 721 [16]. These are photographs of varnished paintings, so the match is to the screen, not to a pigment [16].

The word is steady in print. In Google Books, *brick red* stood at about a third of its peak in 1800 and peaked around 1948 [17].

questions.q: What do Paterson's dictionary and common use disagree about in the word brick-red?
choices: Whether it is orange-leaning (British) or browner and yellower (American)
Whether it is a pigment or a dye
Whether it was named in the twentieth century
Whether it is a warm or cool color
questions.answer: Whether it is orange-leaning (British) or browner and yellower (American)
